tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Walking through the market, the spices smelled amazing.
Packed carefully in tissue paper, Lena carried the fragile vase home.
Hoping for clear skies, the hikers set out before dawn.
Burned on one side, the toast still tasted fine with jam.
Running late for practice, the gym bag was left by the door.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The spices were not walking; the person walking is missing as the subject.

Tip: After a participial opener, the next noun must be the one doing/having that action.

FALSE — Lena was not packed in tissue; the vase was.

Tip: Match the participle to the thing modified: "Packed…, the vase…".

TRUE — The hikers hoped for clear skies, so the opener attaches correctly.

Tip: Ask who or what the -ing phrase describes; that answer should be the grammatical subject.

TRUE — The toast was burned on one side; the participle correctly modifies "toast".

Tip: Past participles often describe a state of the subject (burned, packed, frozen).

FALSE — The gym bag was not running late; the athlete was.

Tip: A dangling -ing phrase needs a person (or agent) as the subject of the main clause.
highlights: Walking through the market, the spices
Packed carefully in tissue paper, Lena
Hoping for clear skies, the hikers
Burned on one side, the toast
Running late for practice, the gym bag
tasks.solution_overview: Scan each opener: the participial phrase must modify the subject that follows. If spices walk or bags run late, the sentence dangles—rewrite so the logical doer becomes the subject.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tired after the long flight, Maya collapsed onto the sofa.
Covered in mud after the match, the boots needed a thorough scrub.
Having lost the map, the trail suddenly seemed endless.
Stirring the soup slowly, a rich aroma filled the kitchen.
Excited about the museum trip, the children packed their sketchbooks.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Maya was tired; the past participle correctly modifies her.

Tip: Adjective-like past participles (tired, excited, frozen) still need a matching subject.

TRUE — The boots were covered in mud; no dangling modifier.

Tip: If the participle describes a thing’s condition, that thing should be the subject.

FALSE — The trail did not lose the map; the hikers did.

Tip: "Having + past participle" still requires the logical agent as subject.

FALSE — An aroma cannot stir soup; the cook is missing.

Tip: Active -ing openers need a person (or agent) who performs the action.

TRUE — The children were excited; the opener attaches cleanly.

Tip: Emotion adjectives from participles (excited, worried) modify people, not places or objects.
highlights: Tired after the long flight, Maya
Covered in mud after the match, the boots
Having lost the map, the trail
Stirring the soup slowly, a rich aroma
Excited about the museum trip, the children
tasks.solution_overview: Task 2 mixes past participles and "having + PP" forms. Correct lines keep agent and participle aligned; wrong ones assign map-losing or soup-stirring to trails and aromas.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Looking out the train window, the countryside rushed past in a blur.
Soaked by the sudden shower, Omar ducked under a café awning.
Written in tiny handwriting, the recipe card was hard to read.
Waiting for the ferry, seagulls circled above the pier.
Finished with homework, Priya started a new puzzle.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The countryside was not looking out the window; the passenger was.

Tip: Sight/perception -ing phrases almost always need a person as subject.

TRUE — Omar was soaked; the participle matches the subject.

Tip: "Soaked/drenched/frozen by…" naturally modifies the person who got wet or cold.

TRUE — The recipe card was written in tiny handwriting.

Tip: Passive sense of the past participle often points to the object described.

FALSE — Seagulls were not waiting for the ferry; the travellers were.

Tip: Location scenes tempt dangling openers—check who waited, not what was nearby.

TRUE — Priya finished homework; "Finished with…" correctly modifies her.

Tip: "Finished with X" works when the subject is the person who finished.
highlights: Looking out the train window, the countryside
Soaked by the sudden shower, Omar
Written in tiny handwriting, the recipe card
Waiting for the ferry, seagulls
Finished with homework, Priya
tasks.solution_overview: Everyday travel and home scenes still follow one rule: the participle’s logical subject must be the sentence subject. Landscape and wildlife openers often dangle unless a person comes next.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having packed the tent, the campsite looked ready for the night.
Cheering loudly from the stands, the fans urged the team forward.
Left overnight in the fridge, the dough rose beautifully.
Reading on the balcony, a cool breeze turned the pages.
Painted bright yellow last spring, the garden shed stood out among the trees.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The campsite did not pack the tent.

Tip: "Having packed…" needs the packer as subject: "Having packed the tent, we…".

TRUE — The fans were cheering; the opener is correctly attached.

Tip: Crowd actions (-ing) belong with people subjects, not the score or the pitch.

TRUE — The dough was left overnight; past participle matches.

Tip: Food prep sentences often use past participles for what happened to the ingredient.

FALSE — A breeze does not read; the reader is missing.

Tip: If the opener is an intentional human action, the subject must be human (or an agent).

TRUE — The shed was painted yellow; no dangling modifier.

Tip: "Painted/repaired/built…" usually modifies the object that received the action.
highlights: Having packed the tent, the campsite
Cheering loudly from the stands, the fans
Left overnight in the fridge, the dough
Reading on the balcony, a cool breeze
Painted bright yellow last spring, the garden shed
tasks.solution_overview: Camping, sports, and kitchen lines: correct ones keep participle and subject paired; wrong ones give packing or reading to places and breezes. Fix by naming the real agent first.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Jogging along the canal path, Sam spotted a heron in the reeds.
Wrapped in a thick blanket, the film felt twice as cosy.
Having trained all week, the final whistle still came as a shock.
Chopped finely and fried gently, the onions sweetened the sauce.
Standing in the doorway, the hallway light cast long shadows.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Sam was jogging and spotted the heron; clean attachment.

Tip: When the same person does both actions, an -ing opener is usually safe.

FALSE — The film was not wrapped in a blanket; the viewer was.

Tip: Comfort/clothing participles modify people or bodies, not the entertainment.

FALSE — The whistle did not train all week; the player or team did.

Tip: "Having trained…" must be followed by the athlete (or team), not a result or signal.

TRUE — The onions were chopped and fried; past participles fit.

Tip: Cooking sequences often stack past participles before the ingredient subject.

FALSE — The hallway light was not standing in the doorway.

Tip: Posture verbs (standing, sitting, leaning) need a person or object that can hold that pose as subject.
highlights: Jogging along the canal path, Sam
Wrapped in a thick blanket, the film
Having trained all week, the final whistle
Chopped finely and fried gently, the onions
Standing in the doorway, the hallway light
tasks.solution_overview: Difficulty steps up slightly: some wrong lines look natural until you ask who wrapped, trained, or stood. Only Sam and the onions keep a logical subject–participle match.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Arriving early at the library, quiet study desks were easy to find.
Frozen solid after the cold night, the birdbath needed warm water.
Hoping to improve her serve, Nina practised against the garage wall.
Filled with fresh berries, Tom carried the bowl to the picnic table.
Turning the page slowly, the mystery finally made sense.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Desks did not arrive early; the student did.

Tip: Time-of-arrival openers need a person as subject, not the place or furniture.

TRUE — The birdbath was frozen solid; past participle fits.

Tip: Weather effects on objects are natural past-participle modifiers.

TRUE — Nina hoped to improve her serve; correct attachment.

Tip: Purpose/hope -ing phrases should be followed by the person with that goal.

FALSE — Tom was not filled with berries; the bowl was.

Tip: "Filled/loaded/packed with…" modifies the container, not the carrier—unless you mean something else.

FALSE — The mystery did not turn the page.

Tip: Reading actions belong with the reader: "Turning the page slowly, she…".
highlights: Arriving early at the library, quiet study desks
Frozen solid after the cold night, the birdbath
Hoping to improve her serve, Nina
Filled with fresh berries, Tom
Turning the page slowly, the mystery
tasks.solution_overview: Watch container vs carrier (bowl vs Tom) and arrival vs furniture. Correct sentences keep frozen birdbaths and hoping athletes as subjects; dangling lines shuffle those roles.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having watered the plants, the windowsill looked bright again.
Stuck in traffic near the stadium, we missed the opening kick-off.
Kneaded for ten minutes, the bread dough became smooth and elastic.
Watching the sunset from the ridge, a silence settled over the group.
Repaired with strong tape, the torn map lasted the rest of the hike.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The windowsill did not water the plants.

Tip: "Having watered…" requires the gardener as subject.

TRUE — We were stuck in traffic; the participle modifies "we".

Tip: "Stuck/caught/trapped…" with a human subject is a common correct pattern.

TRUE — The dough was kneaded; past participle attaches properly.

Tip: Baking steps as past participles usually modify the dough, batter, or loaf.

FALSE — Silence was not watching the sunset; the hikers were.

Tip: Abstract subjects (silence, calm, tension) rarely perform -ing actions in openers.

TRUE — The map was repaired; no dangling modifier.

Tip: "Repaired/mended/patched…" modifies the damaged object.
highlights: Having watered the plants, the windowsill
Stuck in traffic near the stadium, we
Kneaded for ten minutes, the bread dough
Watching the sunset from the ridge, a silence
Repaired with strong tape, the torn map
tasks.solution_overview: Home gardening and trail repairs show the same test: who did the -ing/-ed action? Abstract nouns and furniture as subjects after active openers almost always dangle.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Skipping breakfast before the exam, concentration proved difficult.
Dried on the washing line, the sheets smelled of sunshine.
Having booked the earliest train, Lara reached the coast by noon.
Cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, the desk needed clearing.
Scoring the winning goal, the stadium erupted in cheers.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Concentration did not skip breakfast; the student did.

Tip: Result nouns (concentration, success, fatigue) cannot be the agent of the opener.

TRUE — The sheets were dried on the line; correct.

Tip: "Dried/hung/aired…" naturally modifies laundry or similar objects.

TRUE — Lara booked the train; "Having booked…" fits.

Tip: Travel logistics with "having + PP" need the traveller as subject.

TRUE — The desk was cluttered; past participle matches.

Tip: "Cluttered/covered/littered with…" modifies the surface or space.

FALSE — The stadium did not score the goal; the player did.

Tip: Sports highlights often dangle when the venue follows a player’s action.
highlights: Skipping breakfast before the exam, concentration
Dried on the washing line, the sheets
Having booked the earliest train, Lara
Cluttered with textbooks and notebooks, the desk
Scoring the winning goal, the stadium
tasks.solution_overview: Study, laundry, travel, and sports: three lines attach correctly to sheets, Lara, and the desk. The danglers assign breakfast-skipping and goal-scoring to concentration and a stadium.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Shivering in the queue for tickets, hot tea sounded irresistible.
Grown in the neighbour’s garden, the tomatoes were unusually sweet.
Having finished the crossword, Eli started a new novel.
Hidden behind the sofa cushions, the remote finally turned up.
Cycling through the park at dusk, streetlamps flickered on one by one.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Hot tea was not shivering in the queue.

Tip: Sensory desires as subjects after bodily -ing phrases usually create danglers.

TRUE — The tomatoes were grown in the garden; correct.

Tip: "Grown/picked/harvested…" modifies the produce.

TRUE — Eli finished the crossword; attachment is clear.

Tip: "Having finished X" + person subject is a reliable pattern.

TRUE — The remote was hidden; past participle fits.

Tip: Lost-and-found household items often take "hidden/buried/tucked…".

FALSE — Streetlamps were not cycling through the park.

Tip: Motion openers need the cyclist, walker, or runner as subject—not the scenery.
highlights: Shivering in the queue for tickets, hot tea
Grown in the neighbour’s garden, the tomatoes
Having finished the crossword, Eli
Hidden behind the sofa cushions, the remote
Cycling through the park at dusk, streetlamps
tasks.solution_overview: Mid-difficulty danglers look vivid (shivering → tea; cycling → lamps). Keep asking: can this subject literally do or undergo the participle’s action?

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Burned at the edges but soft in the centre, the cookies disappeared fast.
Listening carefully to the podcast, the recipe steps became clear.
Having lost his gloves, Noah kept his hands in his pockets.
Stacked neatly beside the door, the hiking boots waited for the weekend.
Crossing the busy square, a street musician started a lively tune.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The cookies were burned at the edges; past participle matches.

Tip: Descriptive food states before the food noun are usually correct.

FALSE — Recipe steps do not listen to podcasts.

Tip: "Listening/watching/reading…" needs a person (or animal) subject.

TRUE — Noah lost his gloves; "Having lost…" is correctly attached.

Tip: Possession loss with "having lost" must be followed by the owner.

TRUE — The boots were stacked neatly; correct.

Tip: Arrangement participles (stacked, lined, arranged) modify the arranged items.

FALSE — The musician may have been in the square, but "Crossing…" currently modifies him wrongly if he was already there—and grammatically the subject is said to be crossing while starting a tune in an odd attach; more clearly: if the walker crossed, the subject should be the walker.

Tip: Who crossed? Put that person (not the musician already performing) as subject—or rewrite without the opener.
highlights: Burned at the edges but soft in the centre, the cookies
Listening carefully to the podcast, the recipe steps
Having lost his gloves, Noah
Stacked neatly beside the door, the hiking boots
Crossing the busy square, a street musician
tasks.solution_overview: Food and home lines are mostly solid; the danglers pair listening with steps and crossing with a musician who is not clearly the crosser. Reattach openers to the real agent.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having climbed the spiral staircase, the attic smelled of old cedar.
Rinsed under cold water, the salad leaves stayed crisp.
Worried about the weather forecast, the picnic basket stayed packed indoors.
Sliding into third base, the umpire called him safe.
Printed on recycled paper, the flyer advertised the school concert.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The attic did not climb the staircase.

Tip: "Having climbed…" needs the climber as subject.

TRUE — The leaves were rinsed; past participle fits.

Tip: Prep verbs on ingredients (rinsed, peeled, sliced) modify the food.

FALSE — The picnic basket was not worried; the hosts were.

Tip: Emotion participles (worried, delighted, annoyed) modify people, not objects.

FALSE — The umpire did not slide into third; the runner did.

Tip: Sports action openers must be followed by the player who performed the move.

TRUE — The flyer was printed on recycled paper; correct.

Tip: "Printed/published/posted…" usually modifies the document or notice.
highlights: Having climbed the spiral staircase, the attic
Rinsed under cold water, the salad leaves
Worried about the weather forecast, the picnic basket
Sliding into third base, the umpire
Printed on recycled paper, the flyer
tasks.solution_overview: Emotion and sports danglers are easy to miss: baskets do not worry, umpires do not slide. Keep mental states and athletic moves attached to people.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Folded into neat squares, the napkins brightened the dinner table.
Having studied until midnight, the exam questions still felt unfamiliar.
Dripping from the eaves after the storm, the rain barrel filled quickly.
Searching for a quiet café, the guidebook recommended three streets nearby.
Exhausted but pleased, the choir packed away the music stands.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The napkins were folded; past participle matches.

Tip: Household "folded/ironed/pressed…" modifies the fabric item.

FALSE — Exam questions did not study until midnight.

Tip: "Having studied…" must be followed by the student.

FALSE — The rain barrel was not dripping from the eaves; the water was—or rewrite: "Dripping…, rain filled the barrel".

Tip: Make sure the participle’s subject is what drips, hangs, or falls—not the container alone if the opener describes the water.

FALSE — The guidebook was not searching for a café.

Tip: Search/look-for openers need a person traveller as subject.

TRUE — The choir was exhausted but pleased; correct.

Tip: Paired emotion adjectives still require a human (or animate) subject.
highlights: Folded into neat squares, the napkins
Having studied until midnight, the exam questions
Dripping from the eaves after the storm, the rain barrel
Searching for a quiet café, the guidebook
Exhausted but pleased, the choir
tasks.solution_overview: Only napkins and choir keep solid matches. Study, weather, and travel danglers assign human actions to questions, barrels, and guidebooks—rewrite with the real agent.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Seasoned generously with herbs, the roast chicken came out of the oven golden.
Having missed the last bus, the walk home took nearly an hour.
Balanced carefully on the windowsill, the orchid tilted toward the light.
Cheering for their classmates, the relay baton felt heavier than usual.
Written by a local poet, the short story won the school prize.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — The chicken was seasoned; past participle fits.

Tip: Seasoned/marinated/basted modifies the dish.

FALSE — The walk did not miss the bus; the traveller did.

Tip: "Having missed…" needs a person subject, not the resulting journey.

TRUE — The orchid was balanced on the sill; correct.

Tip: Position participles can modify plants and objects that sit or rest.

FALSE — The baton was not cheering.

Tip: Spectator -ing openers need people (fans, classmates), not equipment.

TRUE — The short story was written by a local poet; correct.

Tip: "Written by…" almost always modifies the text or work.
highlights: Seasoned generously with herbs, the roast chicken
Having missed the last bus, the walk home
Balanced carefully on the windowsill, the orchid
Cheering for their classmates, the relay baton
Written by a local poet, the short story
tasks.solution_overview: Higher difficulty: results ("the walk") and gear ("the baton") look related to the scene but cannot perform the participle. Keep "having missed" and cheering with people.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tangled in the blackberry bushes, the path seemed to disappear.
Having tuned the guitar carefully, the first chord rang clear.
Glazed with honey and nuts, the pastry cooled on a wire rack.
Running to catch the tram, her scarf slipped from her shoulders.
Stored in a cool cupboard, the spices kept their aroma for months.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The path was not tangled in bushes; a person or animal might have been—or the bushes tangled something else.

Tip: If "tangled" describes a hiker’s state, make the hiker the subject.

FALSE — The chord did not tune the guitar.

Tip: "Having tuned…" needs the musician as subject.

TRUE — The pastry was glazed; past participle matches.

Tip: Baking finishes (glazed, dusted, iced) modify the baked good.

FALSE — Classic dangler: the scarf was not running; she was. (Also, "her scarf" as subject after "Running…" wrongly says the scarf ran.)

Tip: Possessive subjects after -ing openers often create dangling modifiers—name the person first.

TRUE — The spices were stored cool; correct.

Tip: Storage participles modify the stored items.
highlights: Tangled in the blackberry bushes, the path
Having tuned the guitar carefully, the first chord
Glazed with honey and nuts, the pastry
Running to catch the tram, her scarf
Stored in a cool cupboard, the spices
tasks.solution_overview: Nature and music danglers are subtle; the scarf line is a classic possessive trap. Only pastry and spices keep a clean participle–subject link.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having stirred the sauce for twenty minutes, a silky texture finally appeared.
Pinned to the noticeboard, the timetable showed every club meeting.
Leaning over the garden fence, neighbours swapped seeds and tips.
Defeated in the first set, the second set still offered hope.
Carved from a single piece of wood, the salad bowl felt smooth to the touch.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A texture did not stir the sauce.

Tip: Cooking "having + PP" openers need the cook as subject.

TRUE — The timetable was pinned up; correct.

Tip: "Pinned/posted/taped…" modifies the notice or paper.

TRUE — Neighbours were leaning and swapping; -ing attaches to people.

Tip: Shared activities work when the subject group performs the opener’s action.

FALSE — The second set was not defeated; the player was.

Tip: Match outcome participles (defeated, exhausted) to the competitor, not the next phase.

TRUE — The bowl was carved from wood; past participle fits.

Tip: Craft/make participles modify the finished object.
highlights: Having stirred the sauce for twenty minutes, a silky texture
Pinned to the noticeboard, the timetable
Leaning over the garden fence, neighbours
Defeated in the first set, the second set
Carved from a single piece of wood, the salad bowl
tasks.solution_overview: Results and next stages (texture, second set) tempt danglers after cooking and sports openers. Keep agents human; let objects take only state/make participles that truly describe them.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Wading into the cold lake, goosebumps rose along her arms.
Annotated in the margins, the textbook looked well used.
Having repaired the puncture, the bicycle was ready for the trail.
Sipping tea on the porch, evening birdsong filled the garden.
Buried under last year’s leaves, the garden path was hard to find.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Goosebumps were not wading into the lake.

Tip: Bodily reactions as subjects after motion openers almost always dangle—use "she" as subject.

TRUE — The textbook was annotated; correct.

Tip: Study participles (annotated, highlighted, dog-eared) modify the book.

TRUE — Acceptable: the bicycle (or its tyre) is what was repaired in effect; more precisely, many style guides allow this when the object was repaired—"Having repaired the puncture, she…" is safer, but "the bicycle was ready" after repairing its puncture is widely accepted as logical for the bike’s state.

Tip: Prefer the person who repaired it if you want the safest formal reading; here the intended reading is that the bike (post-repair) is ready—treated as TRUE for logical object focus.

FALSE — Birdsong was not sipping tea.

Tip: Leisure -ing openers need a person subject.

TRUE — The path was buried under leaves; past participle matches.

Tip: "Buried/hidden/covered…" can modify places and paths.
highlights: Wading into the cold lake, goosebumps
Annotated in the margins, the textbook
Having repaired the puncture, the bicycle
Sipping tea on the porch, evening birdsong
Buried under last year’s leaves, the garden path
tasks.solution_overview: Body reactions and nature sounds create vivid danglers. Object-focused past participles on books, bikes, and paths are fine when the participle truly describes that object.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having tasted every sample at the food fair, the decision became impossible.
Polished until it shone, the trophy sat on the top shelf.
Dashing through the rain toward the pavilion, umbrellas were useless against the wind.
Layered with cream and strawberries, the cake barely fitted in the fridge.
Confused by the trail markers, the map seemed to contradict itself.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The decision did not taste the samples.

Tip: "Having tasted…" needs the eater as subject.

TRUE — The trophy was polished; correct.

Tip: "Polished/cleaned/buffed…" modifies the object treated.

FALSE — Umbrellas were not dashing through the rain.

Tip: Motion openers need the people running; equipment cannot be the agent here.

TRUE — The cake was layered; past participle fits.

Tip: Construction participles for food (layered, filled, topped) modify the dish.

FALSE — The map was not confused; the hiker was.

Tip: Mental-state participles modify people—even when a map is involved in the confusion.
highlights: Having tasted every sample at the food fair, the decision
Polished until it shone, the trophy
Dashing through the rain toward the pavilion, umbrellas
Layered with cream and strawberries, the cake
Confused by the trail markers, the map
tasks.solution_overview: Hard danglers hide behind related nouns (decision, umbrellas, map). Only trophy and cake undergo the participle’s action or state directly.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Twisting the radio dial slowly, a faint station finally came through.
Packed the night before, the suitcase stood ready by the door.
Having overwatered the ferns, yellow leaves began to drop.
Stretching after yoga class, the wooden floor felt warm underfoot.
Signed by every teammate, the jersey became a keepsake.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A station did not twist the dial.

Tip: Instrument/action openers need the person handling the object.

TRUE — The suitcase was packed; correct.

Tip: Travel "packed/zipped/labelled…" modifies the bag or case.

FALSE — Yellow leaves did not overwater the ferns.

Tip: "Having overwatered…" needs the gardener; then you can mention the leaves in a new clause.

FALSE — The floor was not stretching after yoga.

Tip: Exercise -ing openers require the person stretching.

TRUE — The jersey was signed; past participle matches.

Tip: "Signed/inscribed/embroidered…" modifies the item that received the mark.
highlights: Twisting the radio dial slowly, a faint station
Packed the night before, the suitcase
Having overwatered the ferns, yellow leaves
Stretching after yoga class, the wooden floor
Signed by every teammate, the jersey
tasks.solution_overview: Hobbies and home care produce near-miss subjects (station, leaves, floor). Ask whether the subject could perform or receive the participle’s action; only suitcase and jersey pass.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Flying low over the marsh, a sudden gust rocked the small plane.
Simmered for hours with garlic and thyme, the stew filled the kitchen with warmth.
Having forgotten her locker key, the PE kit stayed behind the door.
Crouched beside the stream, the photographer waited for the kingfisher.
Scattered across the rug, building blocks made evening clear-up slow.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A gust was not flying the plane; the plane (or pilot) was flying—rewrite so "the plane" or "we" follows "Flying…".

Tip: After "Flying…", the next noun should be the aircraft or pilot, not the weather.

TRUE — The stew was simmered; past participle fits.

Tip: Long cooking processes as past participles modify the dish.

FALSE — The PE kit did not forget the key.

Tip: "Having forgotten…" needs the person; then mention the kit separately.

TRUE — The photographer was crouched and waiting; correct.

Tip: Posture + person subject is a reliable non-dangling pattern.

TRUE — The blocks were scattered; past participle matches.

Tip: "Scattered/strewn/spread…" modifies the items in that state.
highlights: Flying low over the marsh, a sudden gust
Simmered for hours with garlic and thyme, the stew
Having forgotten her locker key, the PE kit
Crouched beside the stream, the photographer
Scattered across the rug, building blocks
tasks.solution_overview: Nature and school scenes: weather and kit cannot fly or forget. Correct lines keep stew, photographer, and blocks as the true subjects of their participles.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having measured the ingredients twice, a perfect loaf seemed guaranteed.
Mended with invisible thread, the costume survived the whole play.
Peeking through the kitchen blinds, the smell of fresh bread drifted in.
Drenched after the charity run, the volunteers shared orange slices.
Built into the hillside, the cabin stayed cool even in midsummer.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A loaf (or the guarantee) did not measure the ingredients.

Tip: "Having measured…" needs the baker as subject.

TRUE — The costume was mended; past participle fits.

Tip: Repair participles modify the repaired clothing or prop.

FALSE — A smell cannot peek through blinds.

Tip: Perception -ing openers need a person looking or listening.

TRUE — The volunteers were drenched; correct attachment.

Tip: Weather/state past participles (drenched, chilled) with people subjects are clean.

TRUE — The cabin was built into the hillside; correct.

Tip: Construction participles (built, nestled, carved) often modify buildings and places.
highlights: Having measured the ingredients twice, a perfect loaf
Mended with invisible thread, the costume
Peeking through the kitchen blinds, the smell
Drenched after the charity run, the volunteers
Built into the hillside, the cabin
tasks.solution_overview: Final set: abstract results and sensory nouns after active openers fail; costume, volunteers, and cabin succeed. Always verify that the subject after the comma is what the participle really describes.
